title: Nusaybah bint Ka'b
hook: who fought at Uhud to shield the Prophet, and was praised by him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl, greeted as a rider come home. Your line was: welcomed like a traveler. Did you leave someone's family past outside the door? Day eight hundred forty-six.

Wherever I turned, to the left or to the right, I saw her fighting to defend me. The early historians put those words in the mouth of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about a day when the lines broke and men ran. The one he saw was a woman of Medina. In the old accounts, she had come to the field to give water to the thirsty and tend the wounded. When the danger reached him, she set the water down and fought. Her name was Nusaybah bint Ka'b, also called Umm Umarah. Today: the woman who stayed when others ran.
screen: `LEFT OR RIGHT, I SAW HER.` → `SHE CAME WITH WATER.` → `SHE SET IT DOWN AND FOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Nusaybah was from Medina, one of the helpers. The biographies place her among those who pledged themselves to the Prophet before he ever came to their city. That day was Uhud. As the early historians tell it, she fought beside her husband and her sons to keep attackers away from him, and she was wounded. Then come the words we started with: left or right, wherever he turned, she was there. Not that she was strong for a woman. That she was there, every time he looked. These accounts come from the sira and the early biographical works, not from Bukhari, so they are told as the historians tell them. There is a second scene, in Tirmidhi, and it's just as brave in a different way. Umm Umarah came to the Prophet and said: I see that everything is for men, and I don't see women mentioned at all. A direct question, to his face. And Tirmidhi reports that in answer, a verse came down, the thirty-fifth of the surah called the Clans. It runs through the believers pair by pair: men who surrender and women who surrender, men who believe and women who believe, the truthful, the patient, the humble, the charitable, the fasting, men and women each time, and it ends with forgiveness and a great reward prepared for them all. So Nusaybah stood her ground twice. Once on a hillside, with a sword. Once in a room, with a question. And the Qur'an itself, reports say, answered the second.
screen: `A HELPER WHO PLEDGED EARLY.` · `THERE EVERY TIME HE LOOKED.` · `WHERE ARE THE WOMEN?` · `MEN AND WOMEN, PAIR BY PAIR.` · then, large: `SHE STOOD HER GROUND.`

segments.voice: The practice: honor a brave woman. Settle, and breathe. Bring one to mind. A mother who held a family together. A nurse on a long night shift. A teacher who stood up for a child. A grandmother who crossed a border with nothing. A friend who asked the question nobody else would. Breathe in, and see her clearly. Breathe out, and say her name, quietly. Then decide how you'll honor her today: a message telling her what she did, or her story told to someone new. If you pray, you can pray for her. The bell holds the time.
Nusaybah, also called Umm Umarah, who fought to defend the Prophet at Uhud when the lines broke, and later asked him where the women were in revelation. Today's word.
Your line: she stood her ground. Today, tell one brave woman, out loud or in writing, exactly what she did that you remember. Day eight hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims tell Nusaybah's story when they remember the women among the companions, and recite Surah al-Ahzab 33:35, which names believing men and women side by side.

options: keep tending the wounded at the edge.
set down the water and fight near the Prophet.

original.note: Arabic: her name as it is usually written.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman who fought in a battle, once.
what it means: she stood her ground twice: with a sword at Uhud, and with a question about where women are in revelation.
what a scholar hears: Tirmidhi's report tying 33:35 to Umm Umarah's question; some narrations give the question to Umm Salamah instead.

sources.ref: Ibn Hisham, Sira; al-Waqidi, Maghazi; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat (Nusaybah at Uhud; 'wherever I turned, left or right, I saw her')

notes: Uhud details (water, fighting beside husband and sons, wounds, the Prophet's praise) are from the sira/Tabaqat; framed as such. Confirm the attribution of the 'left or right' saying.
Her presence at the Aqabah pledge is from the sira; the script says 'the biographies place her among those who pledged'.
Tirmidhi 3211: confirm number and grading. Other reports (e.g. Ahmad, Nasa'i) attribute the question to Umm Salamah; noted in the trapdoor.
33:35 summarized, not quoted; Pickthall's wording was not used to avoid misquoting. Keeper may substitute the exact Pickthall text.
Original: spelling نسيبة; some sources vocalize differently (Nusaybah/Nasibah). Confirm.
